**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The conditions of this flight are **refractive errors** and presbyopia, **night blindness**, **visual field loss**, **vision in one eye only**, **colour vision defects**, **laser injuries** and eye diseases: **glaucoma**, **cataract**, **uveitis**, dry eye and **retinal** diseases. Treatment may be **watchful waiting**, monitoring the prescription and eye pressure; **non-invasive**, with glasses, lenses, eye drops and artificial tears; or **invasive**: **laser** on the cornea or retina, **cataract surgery**, glaucoma and retinal surgery. In a **pressurised** cabin, mild hypoxia already affects night vision. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane without oxygen, night vision worsens above **5,000 ft** at night, and a gas bubble in the eye expands more. In the **helicopter**, instrument vibration and low flying, with wires and obstacles, demand the best acuity and the full visual field.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism and presbyopia have **non-invasive** treatment in most cases: **glasses** or **contact lenses**, reviewed when the prescription changes, with **watchful waiting** between visits. **Invasive** treatment is **refractive surgery** with laser or replacement of the eye's lens, with the waiting periods of the surgery topic (See M2V4 - VIII). The prognosis is good: with the right correction and a spare pair, acuity stays within the standard. In the **helicopter**, vibration blurs instrument reading, and glasses must stay firm under the helmet; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, drier air at altitude and the draught from an open window bother contact lens wearers more.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Poor night vision from presbyopia or an uncorrected prescription improves with **the right glasses**, a **non-invasive** treatment. **Halos** after refractive surgery usually lessen over time, under **watchful waiting**. A **cataract** that dazzles at night is resolved with **surgery**; **night blindness** from retinal disease has no simple cure and makes a crew member unfit. The prognosis depends on the cause. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, anyone flying at night without oxygen above **5,000 ft** loses night vision, and smokers lose it earlier; in the **helicopter** with night vision goggles, the field narrows, and scanning with the head compensates (See M2V4 - IV).

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Field loss from **glaucoma** is treated to stop it from progressing: **eye drops** that lower eye pressure, **laser** and, when these are not enough, **surgery**; the lost field does not come back, and the prognosis depends on starting early. Loss from **retinal** or **nerve** disease follows the cause. **Vision in one eye only** has no treatment that restores depth: management is **adaptation**, for at least **6 months**, with scanning practice (See M2V4 - IV). In the **helicopter** at low level, side scanning for wires and obstacles depends heavily on the field; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane at night, hypoxia narrows the field even further in someone who has already lost part of it.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** **Congenital** colour vision defects have no treatment and do not get worse: management is **watchful waiting**, with practical tests and, when needed, a restriction on the certificate, such as flying **by day only**. Tinted lenses do not correct it and do not count in the exam. An **acquired** defect calls for treating the cause, such as glaucoma or retinal disease, or stopping the medicine that caused it, under medical advice; the effect of sildenafil wears off within hours. In the **helicopter** and the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, which fly more at night at unlit sites and depend more on the lights of other aircraft and obstacles, a night-flying restriction weighs more.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Glare, flash blindness and after-images usually pass within minutes, under **watchful waiting**, with the eye at rest and away from bright light. Anyone who still has a **spot** or pain has their **retina** examined; a retinal burn has no treatment that undoes it, and management is to monitor and protect the eye. The prognosis is usually good, because most effects are temporary, but a retinal injury can be permanent. The **helicopter**, flying low and slowly near cities, stays longer within reach of the laser; on single-pilot flights, there is no one to take over the controls during the flash.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** **Glaucoma** starts with **non-invasive** treatment, the drops that lower pressure, and may need **laser** or **surgery**; a controlled crew member with a normal field can fly. **Uveitis** is treated with **steroid eye drops** and sometimes oral medicine, and flying waits until the inflammation settles. **Cataract** starts with **watchful waiting**, changing glasses, and ends in **surgery** when vision or glare gets in the way. **Dry eye** and **conjunctivitis** are treated with drops. The prognosis is good when treatment comes early; uncontrolled glaucoma and recurrent uveitis are what ground people most. In the **unpressurised** aeroplane and the **helicopter** with an open door, wind and dust irritate a dry or inflamed eye more.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Before surgery, most cases were treated **non-invasively**, with glasses, lenses or drops, and many remain so. The **invasive** procedures in this topic are **refractive surgery**, **cataract surgery**, **retinal** surgery with or without gas and **glaucoma** surgery. After other operations inside the eye or a penetrating eye injury, the UK CAA asks for **1 week** before flying. The prognosis is good when the waiting period is respected; with gas in the eye, flying before it is absorbed can cause blindness. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, the cabin climbs higher and the bubble expands more than in a cabin at 8,000 ft; the helicopter and even a mountain road can expand it, and the surgeon advises on the journey home.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, dur: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before, sleep well, bring up-to-date **glasses** and the **spare pair**, and **neutral gray sunglasses**. During, blink more, use **preservative-free artificial tears** if the eye dries, remove contact lenses if they bother you and do not rub your eyes. At night, use oxygen when the rule requires (See M2V4 - III). After long flights, dry eye usually improves on the ground; pain, redness or blurred vision that do not go away need evaluation (See M2V4 - VII).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Leve ao of: **How to prevent and ease it.** Take to your eye doctor the **distances** you use in the aircraft: panel, overhead panel and charts. Keep the spare pair **in the cockpit**, not in checked baggage. Passengers have no visual acuity requirement, but carry their glasses and prescription in their carry-on bag. A crew member who flies **without the required correction** breaches the certificate restriction: ANAC may ask to see the glasses and the spare pair, and the examiner orders new tests if vision drops or there is eye disease, injury or surgery.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Chegue à a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Arrive at the aircraft with time for your eyes to adapt and avoid strong white light before takeoff. Use the least light that lets you read the instruments and close one eye in front of a landing light. To find something dim, look **off to the side**, 5° to 10°, and move your gaze slowly. In unpressurized flight, use **oxygen** above 5,000 ft at night and do not smoke before flying.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Divida o c: **How to prevent and ease it.** Divide the sky into **10°** sectors and stop **1 second** on each. Every so often, focus on a **distant** point, a cloud, the wingtip, the horizon, to pull the eye out of short focus. Move your **head** to look behind the windshield posts. On climb, descent and near airports, spend more time looking outside.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Saiba seu: **How to prevent and ease it.** Know your result before choosing the career and take the test calmly and in good light. On displays, also check the **shape** and **position** of symbols, not just the color. A crew member who takes sildenafil observes the 8 hours; anyone on hydroxychloroquine or ethambutol has the eye checks the doctor orders.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Faça o con: **How to prevent and ease it.** Keep your glaucoma follow-up up to date, with **visual field** and pressure. Carry your eye drops in your **carry-on bag** and use them on your home schedule, adjusting for the time zone (See M2V8). Do not use antihistamine eye drops right before or during the flight. With a red eye, pain or vision that has dropped, the crew member **does not fly** and the passenger seeks evaluation before boarding. Flying like this risks worsening the eye far from help and, for the crew member, breaching the certificate.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, con: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before, tell the surgeon that you **fly** and ask which **gas** will be used, if any. Schedule the surgery away from your roster and plan the trip home by land if there is gas in the eye. After, **do not rub** the eye, use the drops on schedule and carry the prescription in your carry-on bag. The crew member only returns within their authority's deadlines and, under ICAO, with a review **6 months** later and **every year**.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** A luz fort: **How to prevent and ease it.** Strong **sunlight** calls for the right **sunglasses**. For flying, the lens should filter **70% to 85%** of light, never more; be **neutral gray**, which does not change colors; and block **99% to 100%** of UV. **Polarized** lenses are not suitable, because they black out displays with anti-glare filters and create reflections on the windshield; **photochromic** lenses clear slowly when entering shade. Dark lenses are for **daytime only**.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Some diseases remove one of the three sources of orientation: those of the **inner ear**, such as **positional vertigo**, **vestibular neuritis** and **Ménière's disease** (See M2V3 - III); those of the **eyes**, such as field loss and vision in one eye only (See M2V4 - IV); and those that reduce sensation in the feet and legs, such as **diabetic neuropathy** (See M2V9). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, because neuritis and positional vertigo usually pass, to **non-invasive** treatment, with repositioning manoeuvres, **vestibular rehabilitation** and medicine during attacks, and rarely to **invasive** treatment, such as surgery for resistant Ménière's. Sedating medicines and alcohol make any of them worse. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia above 10,000 ft adds confusion to illusion; in the **helicopter**, low flying, hovering in dust or snow and vibration make disorientation more frequent.
**Treatment, prognosis and type of flight.** Disorientation itself is not a disease: treatment is **training** and procedure. But repeated episodes call for looking for a cause: **inner ear** disease, **vestibular migraine**, medicines, alcohol, fatigue or sleep apnoea. Management is **watchful waiting** when the episode was single and explained by the situation, and **non-invasive** when there is a cause: vestibular rehabilitation, changing the medicine, treating sleep. The prognosis is good when the cause is treated and the pilot practises instrument flying. A crew member with **recurrent** disorientation or vertigo is grounded until assessed. In the **helicopter**, the risk is greater, with low flying, hovering in dust or snow and many single-pilot operations; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, lack of oxygen above 10,000 ft without a mask worsens judgement.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Mild motion sickness calls for **watchful waiting** and habits: seat, horizon, light meal; it usually improves with **habituation**, repeated exposure to flying. **Non-invasive** treatment is medicine taken beforehand and, for the student pilot who gets very sick, a gradual **adaptation** programme with the instructor. There is no invasive treatment for motion sickness; vertigo from disease follows the cause (See M2V3 - III). The prognosis is good: airsickness usually decreases with flying hours. In the **helicopter** and the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, which fly lower and feel turbulence more, airsickness is more common than in the airliner, which cruises above much of the bad weather.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, check the weather and visibility en route and at the destination, and sleep well. During the flight, keep a reference: the **horizon** outside or the **attitude indicator** on the panel, and do not mix the two when the horizon disappears. Avoid abrupt **head** movements in a turn. Passengers who get sick look far away, out the window, instead of reading.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Acredite n: **How to prevent and ease it.** Believe the **attitude indicator**, not your body, and wait for the sensations to pass. On takeoff and go-around without visibility, follow attitude and vertical speed, not the nose-up feeling. In a turn, do not lower or turn your head; if you need to pick something up, level first. Against flicker, do not look through the propeller, vary the RPM and, inside cloud, turn off the anti-collision light and tell ATC.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Estude o a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Study the airport beforehand: runway width and slope, surrounding terrain, lights. When arriving at an unfamiliar airport, look it over from above before landing. Always use the electronic glide slope or the PAPI, and check altitude and distance. Do not fix your gaze on an isolated light in the dark. When in doubt about position or height, **go around**.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Reconheça: **How to prevent and ease it.** Recognize the conflict and say it out loud. Look at the **attitude indicator** and **level the wings** first, then correct pitch and power. If there is another pilot, **hand over the controls**: the two rarely have the same illusion. Tell ATC. After the flight, report the episode; an honest report helps prevent the next one.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Uma vez po: **How to prevent and ease it.** Once a year, take an illusion demonstration in a simulator or with an instructor. Keep instrument and night flying training current. Before each flight, assess the weather and have an exit plan, including turning back, if the weather closes in. In flight, keep your head still in turns and your eyes on the panel when the horizon disappears.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Escolha um: **How to prevent and ease it.** Choose a seat near the wings and by the window; sleep well beforehand; eat light and avoid alcohol. In flight, look far away, rest your head and do not read in turbulence; tell the crew if you feel sick. Passengers who take medication take it before boarding and do not drive afterwards. Crew members do not use drowsy medication and talk to the examiner if the sickness persists.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases of this flight are **epilepsy**, **fainting**, **migraine**, **stroke** and transient ischaemic attack, **head injury** with **brain surgery** and **degenerative** diseases, such as Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis and dementia. Treatment may be **watchful waiting**, observing after a single seizure or an explained faint; **non-invasive**, with medicines, regular sleep and rehabilitation; or **invasive**: **thrombectomy** in stroke, **aneurysm surgery**, **neurosurgery** for trauma, **epilepsy surgery** and **deep brain stimulation** for Parkinson's and tremor. In a **pressurised** cabin, saturation stays close to 93% at 8,000 ft; in an **unpressurised** aeroplane it falls further at 10,000 ft, and an injured brain has less margin. In the **helicopter**, flickering light through the blades and vibration can be triggers for people with epilepsy or migraine, and with a **single pilot** incapacitation becomes an accident.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** After a **first seizure** with a clear cause and normal tests, management may be **watchful waiting**, without medicine, with observation. Epilepsy is treated **non-invasively** with **anticonvulsants** and regular sleep; when medicines fail, there are **invasive** treatments: **epilepsy surgery**, which removes the point where seizures start, and the **vagus nerve stimulator**. The prognosis depends on control: many people go years without a seizure on medication, and a controlled passenger flies like anyone else; flying requires keeping doses on time across time zones. A crew member with epilepsy remains barred by ANAC. In the **helicopter**, sunlight cut by the blades may flicker in the range that triggers light-sensitive seizures; in a **single-pilot** light aeroplane, a seizure leaves no one to take over the controls.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** An explained **vasovagal** faint calls for **watchful waiting** and **non-invasive** treatment: water, salt when the doctor advises, avoiding triggers and **counter-pressure manoeuvres**, crossing the legs and clenching the hands when the warning comes. When the cause is the **heart**, treatment follows the disease, sometimes with a **pacemaker** or **ablation** (See M2V2 - IV). The prognosis of reflex fainting is good; that of cardiac fainting depends on treatment. On board, laying the person down and raising the legs resolves most cases. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia adds to the fall in blood pressure; in the **helicopter** and the **single-pilot** aeroplane, a single faint at the controls is total incapacitation.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Rare, mild migraine calls for **watchful waiting**: a headache diary and control of triggers. **Non-invasive** treatment uses the attack medicine, taken early, and, when attacks are frequent, a daily **preventive**; those accepted and those banned for crew members vary a lot (See the medicines table in this topic). In resistant cases, there are **injection** treatments, such as botulinum toxin, and nerve blocks, small non-surgical procedures. The prognosis is usually good: many people greatly reduce their attacks with prevention and habits. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia above 10,000 ft can trigger an attack; in the **helicopter**, noise, vibration, sun and light flickering through the blades add triggers.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In the acute phase, ischaemic stroke can be treated with **thrombolysis**, an intravenous medicine that dissolves the clot, or **thrombectomy**, a catheter that removes it; haemorrhagic stroke may need **surgery** or catheter treatment of an **aneurysm**. Then comes **non-invasive** treatment: an **antiplatelet** or anticoagulant, statin, control of blood pressure and diabetes, and **rehabilitation**. In **carotid stenosis**, the neck artery, there may be **surgery** or a **stent**. A TIA calls for rapid investigation, not watchful waiting, because it warns of an approaching stroke. The prognosis depends on the size of the lesion and the recovery; the risk of a new event is higher in the first weeks, which is why IATA asks for oxygen in that period. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane without oxygen, the injured brain's margin is even smaller.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Mild concussion calls for **watchful waiting**: rest, a gradual return to activities and watching for warning signs. **Non-invasive** treatment includes **rehabilitation** for dizziness, memory and attention. Severe cases go to **neurosurgery**: draining a bleed, **craniotomy** and fracture repair, and the air left in the skull afterwards calls for **10 to 14 days** before flying as a passenger. The prognosis of mild concussion is good; in moderate and severe injury, the risk of a late **seizure** weighs for months, and it is what sets the long waiting periods for crew members. In an **unpressurised** aeroplane, air in the skull expands more than in a pressurised cabin; in the **helicopter**, vibration and noise worsen the headache and dizziness of post-concussion syndrome.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Many of these diseases start with **watchful waiting**, following function at each visit. **Non-invasive** treatment is the mainstay: **levodopa** and other medicines in Parkinson's, the drugs that change the course of **multiple sclerosis**, beta-blockers for tremor, plus **physiotherapy** and occupational therapy. In selected cases of Parkinson's and tremor that do not respond to medicines, **deep brain stimulation**, with electrodes implanted in the brain, is the **invasive** treatment. The prognosis is one of progression, fast in some and slow in others, and a crew member's flying depends on function remaining stable. For passengers, long flights, time zones and confinement weigh more than the type of aircraft; in the **helicopter** and the light aeroplane, boarding and tight space require more help.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, **d: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before, **sleep well**, eat and drink water; carry your medicines in your **carry-on bag**, with the schedule adjusted to the time zone (See M2V8). During the flight, drink water, avoid **alcohol**, stand up slowly and do not stay on your feet in the aisle for long. If dizziness, aura, weakness on one side or confusion appears, **sit down and tell the crew** right away. Crew members do not fly with a sleep debt or with medicines that cause drowsiness.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, com: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before, eat something and drink water; avoid alcohol the night before and on board. During the flight, move your legs while seated, drink water and **stand up slowly**, in two steps. At the first sign of the prodrome, **sit or lie down** with your legs raised and tell the crew; do not try to reach the lavatory. Anyone who has fainted before should ask for an **aisle seat** and tell the doctor before the trip.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes, dur: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before, sleep, eat and drink water; avoid your known triggers and red wine. Carry the rescue medicine in your **carry-on bag** and take it at the **start** of the pain. On board, use earplugs or headphones against the noise, sunglasses or an eye mask, and do not skip meals. Crew members use only accepted medicines and respect the waiting time after the dose.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The mental disorders that weigh most on flying are **depression**, **anxiety** and **fear of flying**, **bipolar disorder** and the **psychoses**, and the use of **alcohol** and other substances. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, with follow-up in mild stress reactions, to **non-invasive** treatment, which resolves most cases: **psychotherapy**, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, and medicines. **Invasive** treatment is rare and kept for severe cases: **hospital admission** and **electroconvulsive therapy**, given under anaesthesia. Treated early, the disorder usually allows a return to flying; hidden, it gets worse and grounds for longer. In the **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia above 10,000 ft adds slowness to reasoning; in the **helicopter**, many operations have a single pilot, and the restriction to fly with a co-pilot, common in certification, cannot be met.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild depression and stress reactions, management can be **watchful waiting**, with follow-up. **Non-invasive** treatment is the basis: **psychotherapy**, which also treats **fear of flying** and panic, and an **antidepressant**, preferably an **SSRI**. **Invasive** treatment, **electroconvulsive therapy**, is kept for severe or resistant depression; for a crew member, having had it **excludes** the antidepressant pathway through the FAA examiner, and the decision goes to the authority. The crew member's time limits: changing the dose grounds; when stopping the medicine, ground during the withdrawal and another **2 weeks** (ICAO), or **60 days** off the medicine (FAA); anxiety calls for **6 months** without symptoms and without medicine. A passenger in crisis or with thoughts of death **postpones** the trip and seeks help. The ICAO accepts a stable SSRI with a restriction to fly with a co-pilot; in the single-pilot **helicopter** and the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, that restriction often cannot be met.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Bipolar disorder and the psychoses have no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment is continuous, with a **mood stabiliser**, such as **lithium**, or an **antipsychotic**, and psychotherapy. **Invasive** treatment is **hospital admission** during a crisis and, in severe cases, **electroconvulsive therapy**. For the passenger, the prognosis in flight depends on **stability**: someone stable flies; someone in crisis, agitated or at risk to self or others **postpones** until discharge and clearance by the psychiatrist. Lithium calls for extra care: **dehydration** can lead to **toxicity** from the medicine, so drink water and avoid alcohol in flight. Anyone on a depot antipsychotic arranges the injection date around the trip. For the crew member, a brief psychosis can be cleared after **1 year** stable without antipsychotics; mania leads to long-term disqualification. In the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, there is no cabin crew to help in a crisis.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** With occasional use, management is a matter of habit: respect the time limits and do not drink before flying. In **dependence**, treatment begins with **detoxification**, which the passenger should complete **before** travelling, because **withdrawal** also causes on-board emergencies. It continues with **non-invasive** treatment, with psychotherapy, groups and **total abstinence**, and sometimes with **inpatient treatment**, of at least **28 days** in the HIMS programme. The prognosis is good with follow-up: programmes with colleagues, company, doctor and authority return pilots to flying in **3 to 4 months**, with follow-up for at least **2 years**. In the **pressurised** cabin, in a chamber study, people who slept after drinking spent **201 of 240 minutes** with oxygen saturation below **90%**. In the **unpressurised** aeroplane above 10,000 ft, hypoxia adds to alcohol in impairing judgement; in the **helicopter**, the same **8 hours** and **0.04 g/dL** apply.
**Tratamentos e a avaliação.** Estar em: **Treatments and the assessment.** Being in treatment does not fail anyone on its own. **Psychotherapy**, a **non-invasive** treatment, is encouraged by the FAA when appropriate and counts in your favour when reported. **Medicines** must be declared: an antidepressant follows the authority's protocol, and a sedative calls for an interval before flying. **Invasive** treatments, such as **electroconvulsive therapy** and psychiatric **hospital admission**, call for a psychiatrist's report and a decision by the authority before returning to flying. The career prognosis is better for those who declare: a problem disclosed, with the doctor's report, becomes follow-up; a hidden one becomes a violation. The assessment is the same for those who fly a **pressurised** aeroplane, an **unpressurised** one or a **helicopter**; what changes is the class of certificate.
**Tratamento, retorno e tipo de voo.** O: **Treatment, return and type of flight.** Peer support does not replace treatment: it **refers**. From there the colleague goes on to what the case needs: **watchful waiting**, with listening and follow-up, in life crises such as bereavement and separation; **non-invasive** treatment, with psychotherapy and medicine, in depression and anxiety; and, in severe cases, **hospital admission** or a dependence programme. The prognosis is good: when pilots learned that treatment did not end a career, colleagues began to help instead of covering up. The return to flying follows the **time limit** of each disorder and the examiner's decision. In European **pressurised** airline flying, the peer programme has been mandatory since 2021; those who fly alone, in the **helicopter** or the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, have no colleague beside them to notice the change, and the IMSAFE self-check matters even more.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de c: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before every flight, go through the FAA **IMSAFE** checklist: illness, medication, stress, alcohol in the last 24 hours, fatigue, eating and emotion. Do not take your problems into the cockpit: if your head is not in the flight, say so. Sleep, eat and drink water. Anxious passengers plan the trip calmly, keep their treatment up to date and tell the crew if they need help.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Como se pr: **How to prevent and ease it.** How to prepare: sleep well the night before, arrive rested and without alcohol. Bring your doctor's reports if you are in treatment. Answer honestly: the examiner is there to assess the risk in flight, not to judge your life. If you do not understand a question, ask. If the result calls for follow-up, it is usually the way back, not the end of your career.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Como pedir: **How to prevent and ease it.** How to ask for and offer help: if you are not well, talk to someone you trust, to the company or union support programme, or to your doctor. If a colleague is not well, ask, listen and stay with them until help arrives. If there is a risk of suicide, seek help immediately: in Brazil, **CVV** answers on **188**, free, 24 hours a day; in an emergency, **SAMU**, on 192.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The sleep disorders that weigh most on flying are **insomnia**, **sleep apnoea**, **narcolepsy** and **hypersomnia**, **periodic limb movements** and **jet lag**. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, because the insomnia of a trip and jet lag usually pass in days, to **non-invasive** treatment, which resolves most cases: **cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia**, the first choice, **light** at the right time, **CPAP** for apnoea and medicines. **Invasive** treatment is the exception: airway **surgery**, in selected cases of apnoea. In the long-haul **pressurised** jet, time zones, the small hours and the bunk weigh most; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia above 10,000 ft adds to sleepiness; in the **helicopter**, often with a single pilot, there is no one to take the controls if sleep wins.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** A disrupted hormonal clock is not a separate disease: it worsens **appetite**, **blood sugar** and **mood**, and adds to **diabetes** and **obesity** (See M2V9). Management is **watchful waiting** after a single trip, because regular sleep puts the hormones back in place; recovery calls for at least **2 consecutive nights** without restriction. **Non-invasive** treatment is **light** at the right time, low-dose **melatonin**, when indicated, and meal timing; people with diabetes adjust their medicines to the time zone with the doctor. There is no invasive treatment. Those who fly long **pressurised** routes, crossing time zones and nights, shift the hormonal clock more often; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, which rarely cross time zones, what shifts the clock is the early-hours roster.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In travel **insomnia**, management is **watchful waiting** and sleep hygiene. In chronic insomnia, the first-choice **non-invasive** treatment is **cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia**; medicine comes in for a short time, sometimes together with it. In **apnoea**, **CPAP** is the standard treatment, with weight loss and, for some, an oral appliance; airway **surgery** is the **invasive** treatment, for selected cases, and a crew member only returns to flying when treatment proves **effective**. For the FAA, **narcolepsy** and **hypersomnia** are incompatible with crew flying, treated or not; **leg movements** are assessed case by case, with the medicines and ferritin. A passenger with apnoea takes the **CPAP** and uses it on the **pressurised** night flight (See M2V1 - VII); in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, hypoxia above 10,000 ft adds to the pauses; in the single-pilot **helicopter**, untreated sleepiness has no one to cover it.
**Treatment, prognosis and type of flight.** Jet lag calls for **watchful waiting** when the trip is short: you stay on home time and the body never really shifts. On long trips, treatment is **non-invasive**: **light** at the right time, low-dose **melatonin**, short naps and, for a few nights, a **sleeping pill** with medical advice. There is no invasive treatment. The prognosis is good: the clock adjusts about **1 hour per day** after flying east and **1.5 hours per day** after flying west. Anyone on medicines at fixed times adjusts the doses with the doctor. Jet lag is a problem of the long-haul **pressurised** jet; the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter** rarely cross time zones, and in them tiredness comes from the small hours and the duty period (See M2V8 - V).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de u: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before a long trip, decide whether you will adapt or stay on home time: under 2 days, stay on home time. Flying **east**, bring sleep forward and seek morning light; flying **west**, push sleep later and use the late-afternoon light. Do not drive while sleepy on the first day. The full plan is in the next topic (See M2V8 - IV).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Como usar: **How to prevent and ease it.** Using the clock to your advantage: sleep need varies from person to person, but nobody can train themselves to need less: losing a few hours a night already impairs performance after **2 or 3 days**. With **age**, sleep quality worsens, and the same hours yield lighter sleep. The clock's day has strong and weak hours: performance is worst between **1 and 5 a.m.**, the second dip comes in the **mid-afternoon**, and in the hours before bedtime the clock holds wakefulness. Plan sleep, work and demanding tasks with this map in mind.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Como prote: **How to prevent and ease it.** How to protect your hormones: **light** controls melatonin: bright light in the morning and little bright light in the hours before bed. **Growth hormone** depends on the deep sleep of the **early night**, so the first hours of sleep are worth the most. The hunger that appears after short nights is partly **high ghrelin and low leptin**: knowing this helps you not to mistake sleepiness for hunger. Because glucose tolerance is lower **in the small hours**, night workers do better with light meals at those hours and the main meal in the daytime. No supplement replaces sleep: after a few short nights, metabolism already changes.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Outras dic: **How to prevent and ease it.** Other tips: **exercise** increases alertness: preferably outdoors and in daylight, adding the light, but no vigorous effort in the **2 hours before sleep**. Drink **water** on the flight and at the destination: dehydration worsens the symptoms, and **alcohol** and **caffeine** dehydrate; alcohol also makes you fall asleep faster but **fragments** sleep. Take your **bedtime routine** with you. Everyone reacts differently: try the strategies, keep the ones that work for you and remember that **anxiety** and **worries** worsen sleep away from home. The interactive plan above helps you build your schedule.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O sono é a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Sleep is the only cure, and it starts **before the duty period**: before working all night, **sleep during the day**. A **nap of 25 to 30 minutes** before leaving helps; even **10 minutes** already improve alertness. On duty, **caffeine** acts within **15 to 30 minutes** and lasts up to **5 hours**; use it when you need it, not out of habit. **5-minute breaks**, getting up and talking break the monotony, and **controlled rest** on the flight deck is only valid where the authority and the operator allow it. In the small hours, between **2 and 4 a.m.**, double your checks. After the duty period, recover: it takes at least **2 nights** of unrestricted sleep.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Como aprov: **How to prevent and ease it.** Making the most of rest: on a layover, the priority is the **opportunity to sleep**: a dark, quiet, cool room, a reliable alarm and sleep set for the hours when the clock helps. In the US, a crew member who cannot get **8 consecutive hours** of sleep opportunity must **notify the operator**. On board, lie down even if you are not sleepy: the bunk rarely yields more than **5 hours** of sleep, and two periods of **3 to 5 hours** work better than one of 8. On waking from the bunk or from controlled rest, allow **10 to 15 minutes** for inertia to pass before taking over. After runs of night duties or long duty periods, recovery takes **2 consecutive nights** of unrestricted sleep.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Não use re: **How to prevent and ease it.** Do not take a sleeping pill for the first time before a flight, do not mix it with **alcohol**, and do not use caffeine as a substitute for sleep. The doctor asks about **snoring**, **unintended naps** and medicines, applies the **Epworth scale** and, if needed, orders a **sleep study**.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The hormonal diseases that weigh most on flying are **diabetes**, with the risk of **hypoglycaemia**, **thyroid** diseases, **obesity** and, more rarely, the cortisol deficiency of **Addison's disease**, which requires carrying cortisone at hand at all times. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild changes under follow-up, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is the rule: diet, activity, oral medicines, **insulin** and replacement hormone. The **invasive** and ablative treatments are **thyroid surgery**, **radioactive iodine** and **bariatric surgery**, each with its grounding period. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin sits between 6,000 and 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** one, the greater climb enlarges the bubbles in the insulin pump, and above 10,000 ft hypoxia is easily confused with hypoglycaemia; in the single-pilot **helicopter**, the British insulin protocol, which requires a co-pilot, cannot be met.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Diabetes has no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment starts with diet and activity, continues with oral or injectable medicines and reaches **insulin**, by pen, pump or with a continuous sensor. The **invasive** treatment is **bariatric surgery**, which can control type 2 diabetes in people with obesity (See M2V9 - V). The prognosis in flight is good with stable control: the passenger flies, and a crew member not on insulin returns after the waiting period for each new medicine. The grounding periods apply to every **change of medicine**, and a severe hypoglycaemia grounds until assessment. In the **pressurised** jet, long flights call for checking every 4 to 6 hours; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane and the **helicopter**, often single-pilot, there is no one to take the controls during a hypoglycaemia, and the British protocol, which requires a co-pilot, does not apply.
**Tratamentos e tipo de voo.** A insulin: **Treatments and type of flight.** Insulin is the most demanding **non-invasive** treatment for diabetes: pen, **pump** or continuous sensor change the travel routine but do not stop the passenger flying. For a crew member, the FAA requires **7 days** off flying at each change of pump or sensor. Management on the trip is **preventive**: a written plan for the time zone, spare insulin and frequent checks. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin change already alters pump delivery; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, which climbs higher without pressurisation, the pressure change and the bubbles tend to be greater, and it is worth following the pump plan on every climb and descent; in the **helicopter**, repeated climbs and descents call for the same care, and the cold can affect the glucose meter and strips.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **hypothyroidism**, treatment is **non-invasive**: levothyroxine every day, with control tests; the prognosis is excellent, and the return to flying comes with stable function. In **hyperthyroidism**, treatment starts **non-invasive**, with an antithyroid drug and a beta-blocker, and may move on to **radioactive iodine** or **thyroid surgery**, the **definitive** treatments. After them, a crew member stays grounded until recovery and stable function; a passenger follows the team's advice on distance and carries the proof because of airport alarms. With a stable thyroid, the type of aircraft does not change the rule; when uncontrolled, a racing heart has less margin in the hypoxia above 10,000 ft of the **unpressurised** aeroplane, and double vision weighs more in the low flying of the **helicopter**.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** Obesity has a basic **non-invasive** treatment, with diet, activity and, when indicated, a GLP-1-type medicine, respecting the crew waiting periods. The **invasive** treatment is **bariatric surgery**: in the United Kingdom, a crew member is **unfit for up to 3 months** after it, depending on the type of surgery and recovery, with reports confirming full recovery and no incapacitating side effects; **endoscopic** procedures shorten this period considerably. The passenger follows the advice for abdominal surgery, with about **10 days** before flying (See M2V10). Losing weight improves apnoea, blood pressure and blood sugar, and the prognosis in flight improves with them. In the **pressurised** jet, thrombosis on long flights weighs most; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, people with hypoventilation feel the hypoxia above 10,000 ft more; in the **helicopter**, space and weight on board also count in planning.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases in this flight that weigh most on air travel are **anaemia**, **sickle cell disease**, clotting disorders and **thrombosis**, **cancer**, **communicable infections** and reduced immunity, as in uncontrolled **HIV**. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild stable anaemia and sickle cell trait, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: iron, vitamins, anticoagulants, antibiotics, antiretrovirals and chemotherapy. **Invasive** treatments call for an interval before flying: **transfusion**, **surgery**, **biopsy**, drainage and catheter procedures. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin at up to 8,000 ft already reduces the oxygen supply for people with little haemoglobin; in the **unpressurised** one, above 10,000 ft without oxygen, that reserve goes faster, and the small cabin lacks the jet's filtration; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone bleeding or unstable is aeromedical, with a team and oxygen.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild stable anaemia and sickle cell trait, management is **watchful waiting**, with follow-up. **Non-invasive** treatment corrects the cause: **iron**, by mouth or into a vein, vitamin B12 or folic acid, control of bleeding and, in thrombosis, an **anticoagulant** for months or indefinitely. The **invasive** treatments are **blood transfusion**, **endoscopy** or **surgery** to stop bleeding and, in severe embolism, **thrombolysis** or a **catheter procedure**. The passenger's time limits: haemoglobin below **8.5 g/dL**, postpone; sickle cell crisis in the previous **9 days**, postpone; leg thrombosis, fly with stable anticoagulation; embolism, from **5 days** (IATA) or **2 weeks** (British society), with normal oxygen (See M2V2 - VII). In the **unpressurised** aeroplane, without oxygen above 10,000 ft, anaemia and sickle cell disease have less margin; in the **helicopter**, someone who is bleeding travels by aeromedical transport.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In cancer, **watchful waiting** exists: **active surveillance** of some low-risk tumours and follow-up after treatment. The **non-invasive** treatments are **chemotherapy**, hormone therapy, **immunotherapy**, targeted therapies and **radiotherapy**. The **invasive** ones are **surgery**, **biopsy**, catheters and drainage of fluid from the chest or abdomen, and each has its interval: about **10 days** after abdominal surgery (See M2V10), **4 weeks** after removal of the drain from chest surgery and **1 week** after needle lung biopsy or bronchoscopy with biopsy (See M2V1), and **10 to 14 days** after skull surgery (See M2V6). Fever during chemotherapy, bleeding or very low platelets postpone any flight. The prognosis in flight depends on reserve, not on the diagnosis. After surgery, air left in the body expands more in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but the interval applies all the same.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild viral illnesses, management is **watchful waiting**: rest, water and fever medicine, flying only without fever and without breathlessness. **Non-invasive** treatment is an **antibiotic** or **antiviral** when indicated. **Invasive** treatment is kept for severe forms: **hospital admission**, **drainage** of an abscess or of fluid around the lung. Some time limits are clear: in **measles**, isolation lasts until **4 days** after the rash begins, and the return depends on medical clearance; in drug-susceptible **tuberculosis**, flying only after **2 negative sputum smears**, which usually takes about **2 weeks** of adequate treatment; in **multidrug-resistant** tuberculosis, only after **2 consecutive negative cultures**; pneumonia with low oxygen postpones flying (See M2V1). In the **pressurised** jet, filters help but do not protect someone sitting near a sick person; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the cabin is small and the occupants sit very close together.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In HIV there is no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment with **antiretrovirals** is indicated for everyone and kept up without breaks, with prophylaxis when immunity is low. There is no invasive treatment for HIV; procedures come in only for complications. The prognosis is good: with a suppressed viral load, life and travel go on as normal, and the passenger flies without restriction. An active opportunistic infection or very low immunity calls for **postponing** until controlled. For a crew member, the decision belongs to the authority, based on stability and medicine side effects. Altitude and aircraft type do not change the virus: on the long-haul **pressurised** jet, the challenge is the **time zone** in dose timing; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the same medicine and symptom rules apply.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The digestive diseases that weigh most on flying are **reflux**, **gastritis** and **ulcer**; **diarrhoea**, **irritable bowel** and **inflammatory bowel disease**; **hepatitis**, fatty liver and **cirrhosis**; **gallstones** and **pancreatitis**; and **hernias** and abdominal operations. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for symptom-free gallstones, mild irritable bowel and a hernia that does not hurt, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: diet, acid medicines, rehydration, bowel anti-inflammatories and hepatitis antivirals. The **invasive** treatments are **endoscopy**, **keyhole** or **open surgery**, gallbladder removal and, for a failing liver, **transplantation**. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, at 8,000 ft bowel gas grows by about **38%**; in the **unpressurised** one, at 10,000 ft, by about **50%**; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but, as in the light aeroplane, there is almost never a toilet.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild, occasional heartburn, management is **watchful waiting**, with habits. **Non-invasive** treatment is **acid medicine** and, when the **H. pylori** bacterium is present, antibiotics to eradicate it; in the United Kingdom, a crew member is **unfit during eradication** and returns on maintenance medicine. The **invasive** treatments are **endoscopy** to stop bleeding and **surgery** for perforation or stubborn reflux. The crew member's time limits: at the FAA, an ulcer active in the last **3 months** or that bled in the last **6 months** requires proof of **healing**; in the United Kingdom, unfit until recovery and demonstrated healing. A passenger with an ulcer that bled flies only when stable and with adequate haemoglobin (See M2V11 - II). In the **pressurised** jet, gas distends the stomach; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, it distends more; in the **helicopter** and the light aeroplane, a crisis far from a runway has no care.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In mild travellers' diarrhoea and mild irritable bowel, management is **watchful waiting**: water, salts and diet. **Non-invasive** treatment is **oral rehydration**, loperamide when there is no fever or blood, antibiotics in selected cases and, in **inflammatory bowel disease**, bowel anti-inflammatories, immunosuppressants and **biologics**; **steroids** come in during a flare. **Invasive** treatment is **surgery**, such as removing part of the bowel, sometimes with a **stoma**. Crew time limits in the United Kingdom: inflammatory bowel disease only in stable **remission**, and for Class 1, **6 months** in remission on minimal medication, starting with a multi-crew limitation; after removing part of the colon for diverticulitis, at least **3 months**. Anyone with a stoma carries extra bags: gas also fills it on the climb. The **pressurised** jet has a toilet; the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter** almost never do, and a flare becomes an urgent landing.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In isolated test abnormalities and early fatty liver, management is **watchful waiting**, with follow-up. **Non-invasive** treatment is losing weight, **stopping alcohol** and, in hepatitis B and C, **antivirals**, which cure hepatitis C in most cases. The **invasive** treatments are **banding of varices** by endoscopy, **needle drainage** of abdominal fluid, a catheter shunt inside the liver and **liver transplantation**. For a crew member, **oesophageal varices** mean unfit in the United Kingdom; after transplantation, fitness may return with a favourable gastroenterology assessment. A passenger with recent bleeding, new confusion or an abdomen very full of fluid postpones until stable. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin already reduces oxygen for those with little reserve; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft, hypoxia can worsen the confusion of encephalopathy; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone bleeding is aeromedical.

**Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** For **symptom-free gallstones**, management is **watchful waiting**. **Non-invasive** treatment is that of the attack: pain relief, fluids, fasting in pancreatitis and antibiotics for gallbladder inflammation. **Invasive** treatment is **gallbladder removal**, almost always **by keyhole surgery**, and the **endoscopy** that removes a stone from the bile duct. The passenger's time limits: about **24 hours** after a simple laparoscopy and **10 days** after open abdominal surgery (UK CAA). The crew member's: at the FAA, gallstone pancreatitis, single episode, **1 month** after release, with the gallbladder removed and off pain medicine; alcohol-related or recurrent pancreatitis, **3 months** and an FAA decision; in the United Kingdom, symptomatic gallstones mean unfit until removed. The prognosis is good: once the gallbladder is removed, the colic does not return. In the **pressurised** jet, an attack on board calls for a diversion; in the single-pilot **helicopter** and **unpressurised** light aeroplane, sudden pain is incapacitation.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** For a painless **hernia**, management can be **watchful waiting**, and a crew member may be fit; a painful, trapped or femoral hernia means unfit until repaired. **Endoscopy** and **colonoscopy** are short **invasive** procedures: after colonoscopy, with a lot of gas in the bowel, the passenger waits **24 hours**. Simple **keyhole surgery** calls for about **24 hours**; **open** surgery, **10 days**. For a crew member in the United Kingdom, after hernia repair, unrestricted clearance comes only from **3 to 4 weeks**, with adequate recovery. The prognosis is good when the wound has closed, the bowel works and the pain is gone without sedating medicine. Gas left in the abdomen after surgery grows more in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **pressurised** jet, the cabin at 8,000 ft is already enough to hurt; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, but vibration and the effort of boarding weigh on a recent wound.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Each type of hypoxia has its diseases. **Hypoxic** hypoxia comes from **asthma**, **COPD**, **sleep apnoea**, **pneumothorax** and **pneumonia** (See M2V1 - VI to IX); **hypemic**, from **anaemia** and **carbon monoxide** poisoning (See M2V11 - II); **stagnant**, from **heart failure** (See M2V2). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, in a small symptom-free pneumothorax followed with X-rays, to **non-invasive** treatment, which is most of it: **oxygen**, inhalers, **CPAP** and antibiotics. The **invasive** ones are the **chest drain**, lung **surgery** and, in severe carbon monoxide poisoning, the **hyperbaric chamber**. In the **pressurised** aeroplane, the cabin reaches 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** one, supplemental oxygen is mandatory above certain altitudes (See M1V2), and cabin heating from the exhaust can leak carbon monoxide; in the **helicopter**, which flies low, altitude hypoxia is rare, except in the mountains.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** Asthma and COPD have no watchful-waiting option: **non-invasive** treatment is the basis, with maintenance and reliever **inhalers**, **stopping smoking**, **pulmonary rehabilitation**, vaccines and, in advanced COPD, **oxygen**. **Invasive** treatments are kept for severe emphysema: **lung volume reduction**, by surgery or by a **valve** placed during bronchoscopy, and **lung transplantation**; after chest surgery, a passenger waits **4 weeks** after removal of the drain (See M2V1 - VIII), and a crew member depends on the authority's decision. The prognosis in flight is good when the disease is stable. In the **pressurised** jet, those who need oxygen arrange the portable concentrator with the airline; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft without oxygen, saturation falls faster in COPD; in the **helicopter**, flight is low, but cold air and rotor dust can trigger an asthma attack.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In mild apnoea without sleepiness, management can start with habits: **losing weight**, sleeping on one's side and avoiding alcohol and sedatives at night. The standard **non-invasive** treatment is **CPAP**; for some, the **mouth appliance** that moves the jaw forward. **Invasive** treatments are kept for selected cases: **surgery** on the tonsils, palate or facial bones, the implanted **tongue nerve stimulator**, and **bariatric surgery** when there is obesity (See M2V9 - V). After any of them, a crew member only returns with **proven effective treatment**, usually by a new sleep study. The prognosis is good: once treated, sleepiness goes and fatigue risk falls. In the **pressurised** jet, the CPAP goes on board for night flights; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, flights are short and daytime, but sleepiness at the controls adds to hypoxia above 10,000 ft; in the single-pilot **helicopter**, there is no one to take over if sleep wins.

**Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In a small, symptom-free pneumothorax, management can be **watchful waiting**: rest and **follow-up X-rays** until the air is absorbed, sometimes with **oxygen**, which speeds absorption. **Invasive** treatments come in when there is breathlessness or the pneumothorax is large: **needle aspiration**, a **chest drain** and, for recurrence or for those who fly for a living, **surgery**, by **video-assisted thoracoscopy** or thoracotomy, with **pleurodesis** to stick the lung to the chest wall. The time limits are above: 7 days after resolution for the passenger, months and the authority's decision for the crew member. The prognosis depends on surgery: without it, recurrence is the risk that weighs. Trapped air grows by about **38%** at 8,000 ft in the **pressurised** jet and about **50%** at 10,000 ft in the **unpressurised** aeroplane; in the **helicopter**, low flying expands it less, and aeromedical transport of someone with a pneumothorax usually calls for a **drain before take-off**.

Avoid **alcohol and sedatives** for **12 hours** before and during the trip, and carry **batteries for 1.5 times** the journey duration. For crew members, sleep medication has its own rule: the FAA does not allow daily use of sleep aids (See M2V8 - VII).

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Each law has its diseases. Boyle explains **barotrauma** of the ear, sinuses and teeth (See M2V3), **pneumothorax** (See M2V1 - VIII), the gas that distends the bowel after surgery (See M2V10) and the bubble in the eye after retinal surgery (See M2V4); Dalton explains **hypoxia** (See M2V1); Henry, **decompression sickness** (See M1V3 - II). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for a blocked ear that clears by itself in days, to **non-invasive** treatment, with decongestants, nasal steroids and **oxygen**, up to **invasive** treatment: opening the eardrum or placing a **ventilation tube**, **draining the chest** and treatment in the **hyperbaric chamber**. In each case, the time limit for flying is in the flight on that system. In the **pressurised** jet, trapped gas grows **1.4 times** at 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, about **1.5 times** at 10,000 ft and **2.1 times** at 18,000 ft; in the **helicopter**, altitudes are lower, but climbs and descents repeat several times in the same flight.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Dry air aggravates **dry eye**, **rhinitis** and the **dehydration** of those who already drink little, take a diuretic or have diarrhoea. Management is almost always **watchful waiting** and habit: water, less alcohol and caffeine. **Non-invasive** treatment is **artificial tears**, saline in the nose and, for contact lens wearers, switching to glasses on long flights. **Invasive** treatment, **intravenous fluids**, is kept for severe dehydration, which postpones flying until recovery. The prognosis is excellent: symptoms go within hours on the ground. In the **pressurised** jet, long cruise at 10% to 20% humidity dries most; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, flights are short, and what weighs is the heat of a cabin parked in the sun (See M1V4 - I).

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** A cabin at 8,000 ft is harmless for healthy people but weighs on those with little reserve: **COPD** and other lung diseases, **heart failure**, **anaemia**, **sickle cell disease** and **pulmonary hypertension** (See M2V1, M2V2 and M2V11). For them, management can be **watchful waiting** when resting saturation is above 95%; **non-invasive** treatment is **in-flight oxygen**, arranged with the airline beforehand through the **MEDIF**, after a **hypoxic challenge test** when indicated (See M2V1 - IX). There is no invasive treatment for cabin altitude; anyone who does not tolerate it even with oxygen **postpones** the trip until stable. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin stays up to 8,000 ft; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, the cabin is the actual altitude, and the rule requires oxygen from 12,500 ft (See M1V2 - III); in the **helicopter**, almost never pressurised, low flying spares the body, except in the mountains.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** Decompression sickness **has no watchful-waiting option**: even if symptoms disappear on descent, the person is assessed. **Non-invasive** treatment starts in the aircraft, with **100% oxygen** and water, and the definitive treatment is **recompression in the hyperbaric chamber** (See M1V3 - IV), the most intensive treatment, with repeated sessions if symptoms remain. Treated early, the joint form usually heals without sequelae; the nervous system form can leave marks. The time limits: after a rapid decompression in flight, **24 hours** without flying; after chamber treatment, there is no consensus, and advice ranges from **72 hours**, the most cited, to **6 weeks**, with the hyperbaric doctor; a crew member returns only with clearance from the doctor and the authority. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk appears only in decompression; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, on every flight above 18,000 ft; in the **helicopter**, altitude risk is rare, but transport of a sick diver should be as low as possible.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Heat has three steps of illness, and each has its treatment. In **heat stress**, management is **watchful waiting** and habit: shade, a break and water. In **heat exhaustion**, treatment is **non-invasive**: lying down somewhere cool, removing excess clothing, cooling the skin and drinking water with salts. **Heat stroke** is an emergency: **rapid cooling**, preferably in cold water, and **invasive** treatment in hospital, with **intravenous fluids** and monitoring of the kidneys and brain. Anyone who has had heat stroke returns to flying only after recovery and medical assessment; exhaustion calls for at least a day's rest and full rehydration. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk is on the ground, with the cabin parked in the sun; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, the glazed cabin heats up like a greenhouse, the helmet and flight suit hold in heat, and low flying does not cool.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **mild hypothermia**, treatment is **non-invasive**: shelter, dry clothing, insulation and **passive rewarming**, with a hot drink if the person is alert. In **moderate** hypothermia, **active rewarming** of the trunk comes in, with heat blankets and heat in the armpits and chest. In **severe** hypothermia, treatment is **invasive**, in hospital: warmed intravenous fluids and, in extreme cases, **extracorporeal circulation**, which warms the blood outside the body. **Frostbite** of fingers, nose and ears is treated by rewarming in warm water, and **surgery** on dead tissue comes only weeks later, when the limit of the injury becomes clear. The prognosis of hypothermia treated in time is good. In the **pressurised** jet, the risk is a forced landing in a cold region; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, heating is weak; in the rescue **helicopter**, the victim travels **lying down**, warmed and without abrupt movements, because of afterdrop.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases linked to flight radiation are long-term ones: **cancer**, especially skin and breast cancer in studies of crew, and **cataract**. There is no treatment for the dose received; management is **watchful waiting** and surveillance: skin checks, **mammography** and eye examinations at the recommended ages. When disease appears, treatment is that of any case: **non-invasive**, such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy, or **invasive**, such as **cancer surgery** and **cataract surgery**, each with its time limit for returning to flying (See M2V11 - III and M2V4). In pregnancy, protection is **reporting early** and adjusting the roster. In the **pressurised** jet, high, long and polar routes receive the highest doses; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, which fly low, the cosmic dose is much lower, and what weighs is **ultraviolet** through the window.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e tipo de voo: **Treatments, prognosis and type of flight.** In **temporary loss**, management is **watchful waiting**: quiet and protection, and hearing returns within hours. **Noise-induced loss** has no cure; treatment is **non-invasive**: stopping progression with protection and, when conversation becomes difficult, a **hearing aid**. **Sudden deafness**, in one ear, within hours, is urgent: treatment is **steroids** by mouth and, if that is not enough, an **injection into the ear**, an **invasive** treatment; the crew member does not fly until assessed (See M2V3). In profound loss, the **invasive** treatment is the **cochlear implant**. **Tinnitus** is treated with advice, background sound and therapy. The prognosis depends on protecting early: established loss does not come back. In the **pressurised** jet, the cabin is quieter; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane and the **helicopter**, noise exceeds 90 dB, and a **protective headset** is essential.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Vibration is linked to **low back pain** and **neck pain**, and that of maintenance tools to **hand-arm vibration syndrome**, with white, numb fingers. In common low back pain, management is **watchful waiting** and movement: most improve within weeks. **Non-invasive** treatment is **physiotherapy**, exercise, non-sedating pain relief and adjusting the **seat** and posture. **Invasive** treatment, **spinal surgery**, is kept for a disc hernia pressing on a nerve that does not improve, and a crew member returns only after recovery and assessment (See M2V12). The prognosis is good when exposure is cut: seat, posture and breaks. In the **pressurised** jet, vibration is low; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the piston engine vibrates more; in the **helicopter**, the blades vibrate in exactly the band that blurs vision and tires the spine.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** G weighs more on those with **low blood pressure**, **varicose veins**, **dehydration**, **anaemia** or medicines that lower blood pressure, and it injures the **neck** and **spine** of those who turn their head under load. After a G-LOC without injury, management is **watchful waiting**: the pilot recovers within seconds, but the episode is reported and reviewed. The fighter pilot's **neck pain** has **non-invasive** treatment, with **physiotherapy** and strengthening, and only rarely **invasive** treatment, with **surgery** for a disc hernia pressing on a nerve; return to high-G flying depends on recovery and the authority (See M2V12). Anyone who faints without G, on the ground, is investigated before returning (See M2V6 - III). In the **pressurised** transport jet, G barely exceeds 1.5; in the **unpressurised** aerobatic light aeroplane, the pilot almost never has an anti-G suit; in the **helicopter**, G is low, and what injures the spine is vibration and posture (See M1V6 - IV).

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Impact injuries are **spinal fracture**, **fractures** of the arms and legs, **head injury** and injuries to abdominal and chest organs. A **stable wedge fracture** is treated **non-invasively**, with relative rest, a brace and physiotherapy, and grounds the pilot from ejection-seat aircraft for **3 to 4 months** (See M1V8 - III). An **unstable** fracture or one threatening the spinal cord calls for **invasive** treatment: **surgery** with screws and rods. Head injury ranges from **watchful waiting**, in mild concussion, to **surgery** for a haematoma, with its own time limits (See M2V6). Return to flying depends on healing, strength and assessment (See M2V12). In the **pressurised** jet, protection is the **lap belt** over the pelvis and the brace position; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the **shoulder harness**; in the **helicopter**, impact is mainly **vertical**, and energy-absorbing seats protect the spine.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Some diseases make the inner ear even more deceptive: **positional vertigo**, **vestibular neuritis**, **Ménière's disease** and **vestibular migraine** (See M2V3 - III); **alcohol** also alters the inner ear and can keep acting on it after it has left the blood. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, because neuritis usually passes in weeks, to **non-invasive** treatment: a **repositioning manoeuvre** for positional vertigo, **vestibular rehabilitation**, medicine during attacks and migraine prevention. **Invasive** treatment is rare: an **injection into the ear** or **surgery** for Ménière's that does not respond. A crew member with vertigo does not fly and returns only without symptoms, after assessment. In the **pressurised** jet, two pilots and the autopilot give margin to someone who feels disoriented; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the long turn in cloud is the classic trap; in the **helicopter**, head movements and single-pilot flight favour **Coriolis**.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Some eye diseases increase visual illusions: **cataract**, which scatters light and creates glare and halos at night; **vision in one eye only**, which removes part of depth perception; and **weak night vision** (See M2V4). Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for an early cataract that does not yet interfere, to **non-invasive** treatment, with **glasses** of the right prescription and approach training, up to **invasive** treatment: **cataract surgery** and **refractive laser surgery**. In the United Kingdom, a pilot is unfit for at least **6 weeks** after cataract surgery, and refractive surgery requires more than **6 months** and, if requested, a glare test (See M2V4 - VII and VIII). With vision corrected, the prognosis is good. In the **pressurised** jet, instrument approaches and two pilots protect; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the visual night approach is where the **black hole** lives; in the **helicopter**, off-runway landings, in dust or snow, remove the references all at once.
**Tratamentos e volta ao voo.** A desori: **Treatments and return to flying.** Disorientation has no invasive treatment: what is treated is the **cause**. After an isolated, explained episode, management is **watchful waiting**: report, review the flight and train again. **Non-invasive** treatment is **training**: ground illusion demonstrations, simulator and instrument flying with an instructor; for those who get airsick or have a sensitive inner ear, **vestibular rehabilitation**. If the cause is a disease, its treatment comes in, sometimes **invasive**, such as cataract or Ménière's surgery (See M2V5 - II and III), and the return follows that disease's time limit. The prognosis is good: repeated training reduces episodes. In the **pressurised** jet, training is crew training, with task sharing; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the critical point is the pilot without an instrument rating who enters cloud; in the **helicopter**, training includes instrument recovery and landing without references.
**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Repeated hyperventilation usually has a cause: **anxiety**, **panic** and **fear of flying** (See M2V7 - II), but also **asthma**, pain and fever. In an isolated episode, management is **watchful waiting** and breathing: speaking slowly, counting breaths and, above all, checking the oxygen. **Non-invasive** treatment of the cause is **cognitive behavioural therapy**, breathing training and, when indicated, medicine, which has rules for crew (See M2V7 - II). There is no invasive treatment for hyperventilation. The prognosis is good: once anxiety is treated, attacks decrease. In the **pressurised** jet, the anxious passenger has a crew to help; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, above 10,000 ft, hypoxia and hyperventilation are confused, and oxygen comes first; in the **helicopter**, noise, vibration and low flying add stress.

**Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** Those who most need the test and in-flight oxygen have **COPD**, **pulmonary fibrosis**, **pulmonary hypertension**, **cystic fibrosis** or heart disease with little reserve, or have just had **pneumonia**. Management is **watchful waiting** when resting saturation is above 95%; **non-invasive** treatment is **oxygen** in flight, with the flow set by the test, plus treatment of the disease: antibiotics for pneumonia, lung and circulation medicines. The most extreme **invasive** treatment is **lung transplantation**, and after it the return to flying is decided with the transplant team. The prognosis is good when oxygen is arranged beforehand. In the **pressurised** jet, the approved portable concentrator goes in the cabin; in the **unpressurised** aeroplane, the cabin is the real altitude, and oxygen must be available already at lower altitudes; in the **helicopter**, transport of someone who depends on oxygen is aeromedical.
