**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Ajuste o a: **How to prevent and ease it.** Adjust the seat before take-off, with the lower back supported and the arms reaching the controls without stretching. On long flights, stand up and stretch when it is safe. During a flare-up, prefer a simple painkiller and see a doctor if there is numbness or weakness. A crew member taking a medicine that causes drowsiness counts the waiting period before returning to the roster.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, check that the injury is stable and that the cast has been on for the minimum time. During the flight, stand up and move your legs when it is safe, choose an aisle seat and rest your back against the seatback. Carry your daily medicine in your hand luggage and avoid sleeping on a sedating medicine during a long flight. A crew member does not take up duty with pain that limits movement or with a sedating medicine.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Inclua no: **How to prevent and ease it.** Include exercises for the neck, trunk and legs in your weekly training, with professional guidance. Before pulling G, rest your head back and set your gaze; in the helicopter, adjust the goggle counterweight and change posture during breaks. After an injury, return when function has recovered and the examiner agrees.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Peça assis: **How to prevent and ease it.** Request assistance 48 hours ahead, bring your mobility aid and say whether the prosthesis will set off the detector. On long flights, move the joint and check the fit of the prosthesis, which may loosen or tighten with swelling. A crew member brings the functional report to the examiner and, when asked, takes the flight test; any worsening ends the SODA until a new assessment.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Respeite 2: **How to prevent and ease it.** Wait 24 or 48 hours after the cast, depending on the flight length. With a pneumatic splint, let out a little air before the climb. Choose the **aisle**, move your toes and the free knee and walk when it is safe and allowed. Request a wheelchair and assistance in advance. Increasing pain, cold toes or shortness of breath call for help from the crew.
**O passageiro** com deficiência ou mobi: **A passenger** with a disability or reduced mobility is entitled to assistance: ANAC asks for **48 hours'** notice, carries one mobility aid **free of charge** and does not seat that person next to an **emergency exit**. **A crew member** undergoes a functional assessment: ANAC does not accept after-effects that affect safety, and the FAA asks for a report on strength, range of motion and pain and may require a **medical flight test**. Those who pass receive a **SODA**, which does not expire as long as the condition does not worsen.
**O passageiro** com dor sem sinais neur: **A passenger** with pain and no neurological signs can fly, taking care with posture and movement. **A crew member** depends on function: ANAC considers unfit anyone with a **herniated disc with neurological symptoms** or a symptomatic spinal deviation that affects safety. The FAA sends a symptomatic herniation for a central decision; after **disc surgery**, the examiner may clear someone who is **symptom-free, recovered, off medication and without neurological deficit**.
**Para o passageiro**, a maioria das com: **For the passenger**, most airlines wait **24 hours** after the cast for flights of **less than 2 hours** and **48 hours** for longer ones. If the trip is urgent, the cast can be **split open** (bivalved). Anyone injured in the previous **7 days** should contact the airline. **For the crew member**, a limb in a cast or an unhealed fracture is a functional deficiency: controls, pedals and evacuation cannot be guaranteed.
**Para o passageiro**, a pergunta é se e: **For the passenger**, the question is whether they can stay seated, whether the injury swells and whether they can get out of the aircraft in an evacuation. **For the crew member**, ICAO and ANAC look at **function**: there must be no change in bones, joints, muscles or tendons that could interfere with the safe exercise of the licence. After-effects and anatomical defects normally require a **functional assessment**, not just the diagnosis.
**Para o passageiro**, depois de uma les: **For the passenger**, after an injury the treating doctor's rule applies: walking down the aisle, sitting down and standing up and carrying hand luggage without pain. **For the crew member**, the return depends on the examiner: ANAC and the FAA want enough strength, range of motion and coordination for the job, and a military pilot who ejected may be kept off ejection seats for months (See M1V8 - III).
A **amputação**, a **prótese articular**: **Amputation**, a **joint replacement** (such as hip or knee), **osteoarthritis** and **arthritis** have one thing in common: what matters for flight is the **function** that remains. A person with a well-fitted prosthesis may have enough strength and movement; an inflamed joint, without any surgery, may limit more.
A **dor cervical** e a **dor lombar** sã: **Neck pain** and **low back pain** are the most common musculoskeletal complaints among those who fly. Most of the time they come from **muscles and ligaments** overloaded by posture. A **herniated disc** is different: part of the disc moves out of place and can compress a nerve root, with pain running down the arm or leg, **numbness** and **weakness**.
A **fratura** é a quebra do osso; o **ge: A **fracture** is a break in the bone; the **cast** and the **splint** hold the fragments until they heal. In the first hours, the tissue around the injury is still **swelling**. Inside a closed cast, this swelling has nowhere to go and squeezes vessels and nerves. After **orthopaedic surgery**, the wound, the pain and immobility add up.

O **condicionamento físico** é a princip: **Physical fitness** is the main protection for the spine of those who fly. Strong, enduring neck, trunk and leg muscles hold posture for longer, absorb vibration and share the load with the discs. **Return to flying** after an injury follows the same logic: those who return are those who have recovered function, not just those who no longer feel pain.
O **exercício resistido** com elástico,: **Resistance exercise** with elastic bands, done regularly, increased pilots' neck strength and endurance and reduced pain. Other measures help: a **lighter helmet** with well-distributed weight, a **counterweight** for night vision goggles and **positioning the head before** pulling G. A painkiller does not replace training: it removes the pain but does not restore strength.
O **sistema musculoesquelético** sustent: The **musculoskeletal system** supports and moves the body. **Bones** give shape and protect the organs; **joints** allow movement; **muscles** and **tendons** produce force; **intervertebral discs** cushion the load between the vertebrae. In flight, this whole system must hold posture for hours, reach controls and pedals and, in an emergency, get the person out of the aircraft quickly.

**Doenças, tratamentos e tipo de voo.**: **Diseases, treatments and type of flight.** The diseases in this flight that weigh most in the air are **neck and back pain**, **disc hernia**, **fractures**, **osteoarthritis** and **arthritis**, **prostheses** and **amputation**. Treatment ranges from **watchful waiting**, for common pain that improves within weeks with movement, to **non-invasive** treatment, which resolves most cases: **physiotherapy**, exercise, non-sedating pain relief, a **cast** or **splint**. The **invasive** treatments are **spinal surgery**, **fracture fixation** with plates and screws, **hip or knee replacement** and joint injection; the interval after them is set by the surgeon, and a crew member returns pain-free, without sedating medicine and with strength recovered. In the **pressurised** jet, hours of sitting and thrombosis weigh most; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the cramped cabin and the effort of boarding; in the **helicopter**, **vibration** and twisted posture, and in the fighter, the G load on the neck.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** N: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** In neck or back pain without nerve signs, management is **watchful waiting** and active: keeping moving, which usually resolves it within weeks. **Non-invasive** treatment is **physiotherapy**, strengthening and common pain relief; a **muscle relaxant** or an **opioid** grounds for 5 half-lives (FAA). The **invasive** treatments are an **injection** near the nerve and **disc surgery**, for a hernia pressing on the nerve with weakness or pain that does not ease. At the FAA, disc surgery **does not disqualify**: the examiner clears a pilot who is **symptom-free, recovered, off medicine and without deficit**; a hernia with nerve symptoms goes to an FAA decision, and in Brazil means unfit (RBAC 67). The prognosis is good for most. In the **pressurised** jet, getting up and walking helps; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the fixed seat tires; in the **helicopter**, posture and vibration keep the pain going, and night vision goggles weigh on the neck.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e prazos.** A: **Treatments, prognosis and time limits.** An undisplaced fracture may have **watchful-waiting** treatment, with protection and relative rest; most have **non-invasive** treatment, with a **cast**, **splint** or boot. **Invasive** treatment is **surgery**: reduction and fixation with **plates, screws or rods**, indicated when the bone is displaced, the joint is involved or the fracture is unstable. The passenger's time limits: **24 hours** after the cast for a flight under 2 hours and **48 hours** for a longer flight; after surgery, the interval is the surgeon's, and the risk of **thrombosis** weighs in the first weeks (See M2V2 - VII). A crew member returns when the bone has healed and strength and movement allow operating the controls and leaving the aircraft; for a spinal wedge fracture, **3 to 4 months** away from the ejection seat (See M1V8 - III). In the **pressurised** jet, a leg in a cast needs a seat with space; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, the air splint expands more; in the **helicopter**, boarding and vibration hurt a recent fracture.
**Tratamentos, prognóstico e certificaçã: **Treatments, prognosis and certification.** In mild **osteoarthritis** and **arthritis**, management is **watchful waiting** and exercise. **Non-invasive** treatment is physiotherapy, weight control, pain relief and anti-inflammatories and, in arthritis, disease-controlling medicines, some with rules for crew. The **invasive** treatments are joint **injection**, **arthroscopy** and hip, knee or shoulder **replacement**; in **amputation**, stump surgery and **prosthesis** fitting. After a joint replacement, the passenger follows the surgeon's interval and thrombosis prevention; a crew member returns pain-free and with function recovered. For amputation and stable limitation, the FAA can grant a **statement of demonstrated ability**, which does not expire, after a practical test. In the **pressurised** jet, request assistance 48 hours ahead; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, check reach to the pedals and controls; in the **helicopter**, the pedals and collective require both legs and both arms (See the special mission Disability and flying).
**Tratamentos e volta ao voo.** Depois d: **Treatments and return to flying.** After an injury, the return follows steps: relative rest, **rehabilitation** with physiotherapy, strength training and, finally, the practical test of operating the controls and leaving the aircraft. **Non-invasive** treatment is at the centre: **resistance exercise** for the neck and trunk, which also prevents the next attack. When there was **invasive** treatment, such as spinal surgery or a joint replacement, rehabilitation is longer, and a crew member returns only pain-free, without sedating medicine and with the examiner's clearance. The prognosis is good for those who keep training. In the **pressurised** jet, return requires enduring the duty period seated; in the **unpressurised** light aeroplane, strength for the controls and for a quick exit; in the **helicopter** and the fighter, neck endurance against the helmet, night vision goggles and G.
